McCarthy (Calgary). I have an amendment to propose In .connection with the area of land which has been placed under the operation of this Act. If anything further were necessary to show that this government made a mistake in retaining the lands and the natural resources of the western provinces when the Autonomy Bills were submitted to parliament by them, it is the variety of opinion that has been expressed by members on both sides of the House in connection with the administration of those lands. I suppose that 90 per cent of the time of the western members jn this parliament is taken up in looking after business which in the other provinces is dealt with by the local legislatures. The record on the page of * Hansard ' will show that perhaps 50 per cent of the time Of this House has been occupied in discussing western questions which in other provinces are dealt with by the legislatures. At this late hour of the session I do not propose detaining the House at any length further than to refer the Minister of the Interior to what was done by the United States government Mr. OLIVER.
when similar questions came up for consideration there. I would refer him to the United States reports which show that a commission went through the western states of the union and took the evidence of the ranchers and of the farmers and generally of the people interested in the administration of the public lands. I regret that this course has not been followed by the government in the eighteen months interval which has elapsed between the first presentation of this Bill and the present time. I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Roche, of Marquette:
That the said Bill he not now read a third time but be referred back to Committee of the Whole House with instructions to amend the same by providing-
That the Governor in Council shall forthwith issue a commission conferring upon the commissioners therein named power to immediately inquire and report what additional areas (if any) of Dominion lands, should be brought within the provisions of the pre-emption and purchased homestead clauses of the said Bill.
I move this amendment so that the people of the west may have an opportunity of presenting their views with respect to the administration of their lands to the government through this commission.
Amendment (Mr. M. S. McCarthy) negatived on the same division recorded.

I d sire to direct the attention of the House to a subject which was first brought up by the hon. member for Calgary when the Dominion Lands Bill of last year was introduced, and which was again brought to tlie attention of the Minister of the Interior this year when, alfter the session had been six months in existence, he introduced this Bill to the House. I refer to the matter of an endowment for the purposes of higher education in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. If there is one thing upon which people are in accord in this twentieth century it is that the best possible education should be afforded. The foresight of our predecessors has given us an endowment for the purpose of primary education in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. In the province of Manitoba in the year 1885 this parliament provided for the allotment of lands to be set apart and handed over to that province for the endowment of a university. Lands in the two new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan are being disposed of very rapidly, and the day is not far distant when in all probability the public lands in these provinces will have passed into private hands. Especially will that be the case under the provisions of this Bill which we are now about to read a third time. In a new country the needs of development require all the available funds, and consequently there is special need for some reserve fund which may be drawn upon to promote higher edu-

cation. The other universities of the world have been endowed by the generosity of generations of their graduates, but it will be many years before we can look for such gifts for universities in the new provinces of the west. I therefore move, seconded by Mr. Chisholm:
That the said Bill be not now read a third time but be referred back to Committee of the Whole House with instructions to amend the same by providing:
That the Governor in Council shall forthwith institute such proper inquiries as may be necessary for the purpose of ascertaining what quantity of Dominion lands in each of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan should be set aside and appropriated for the purposes of higher education, and that thereupon, after obtaining the consent and approval of the governments of the said respective provinces the Governor in Council shall set aside, appropriate and transfer to the said respective provinces the quantities of said lands so ascertained for the purposes aforesaid.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It seems to me that this amendment, if carried out, will lead to the alienation of public lands, and therefore it is not such an amendment as a private member can move without the consent of the government. My present impression is that it is clearly out of order.

I have only to say that over and over again, in 1905, during the debate on the measures creating the Northwest provinces, motions to the effect that the lands should be transferred to the provinces, instead of being retained by the federal government, were moved by private members and were entertained by the House No such question was then raised, and this is the first time in imy experience that such a question has been raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My impression is that the cases referred to were merely expressions of opinion, and did not take the form of amendments to an Appropriation Act.

Not at all. The hon. Minister of Finance will remember that the Bill then before the House did not hand over the lands to the provinces, and both in committee and on the third reading of the Bill we moved that a clause should be inserted to provide that the lands should be handed over to the provinces. The records of ' Hansard ' and of the Votes and Proceedings will abundantly establish what I say.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should be glad to hear a discussion of the matter by the more experienced members of the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The rule is laid down in sections 53 and 54 of the British North America Act, which are as follows :
53. Bills for appropriating any part of the public revenue, or for imposing any tax or
impost, shall originate in the House of Commons.
54. It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or Bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that House by message of the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address or Bill is proposed.
My Impression is that the public revenue has always been held to include public lands.
If that is the case, the House of Commons transcended its powers in 1905.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It may be that my hou. friend is right, but at all events I think the rule is imperative.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: During the present session hon. members will remember that several petitions were ruled out on the ground that they were presented with the object of alienating public lands. My view has always been tha-t public lands were included under the term revenue, and therefore that a motion or amendment for the alienation of public lands must be introduced, like any money grant, by a resolution which has received the assent of the Crown. In that view I think the latter part of the amendment is out of order.
Does not the latter part of the amendment depend on an inquiry? That is the motive of the motion ; and surely this House can recommend an inquiry without contravening the rules.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: By this resolution, if carried, the House would authorize, not merely an inquiry, but, if the inquiry eventuated in a certain way, an appropriation of public lands.

I think the whole question is whether you would consider this a money vote. There is no doubt that public lands are an asset of the Dominion. I have always had the idea that it required a vote of parliament to alienate public lands. If we pass this resolution, It becomes practically a vote of parliament; it becomes a part of this Act. If it becomes a part of the Act, that Act goes into force when it is assented to and signed.. The point is w'hether it requires the assent of the Crown and introduction by formal resolution. There is a wide difference no doubt between the public revenues and the land assets of the country. Both have values, but they are differently used, and it seems to me that this rule was made with reference to the revenues.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The rule seems to be laid down with fair definiteness at page 028 of Bourinot, where, under the head of ' Appropriation and Taxation Bills,' you will

find tills reference to the Journals of the House of Commons of 1874 :
Since then all grants of public land are initiated in the Commons,
That follows upon a discussion as to the care which the Commons takes not to yield up to the tSenate the initiation of any Bill respecting the expenditure and as to the origin of money Bills. At the moment my view is that the amendment is clearly out of order.

That raises a very important question, Mr. Speaker, because, inasmuch as the Land Bill has not been introduced by resolution, it cannot pass until that resolution has been proposed and the assent of His Excellency thereto has been announced to the House. The position taken by the Prime Minister brings about that situation. It would not be proper,' therefore, to have the Bill read a third time until that assent has been obtained and that resolution has been passed. One position logically follows the other. If land is included in revenue, which is the position taken by the Prime Minister, it is elementary law in this House that you cannot dispose of any part of the public revenue without the assent of the Crown and a resolution of the House. Therefore, if His Honour the Speaker and the Prime Minister are right iu this position, which was not taken in 1905 under similar circumstances, the result is that we cannot pass the third reading of this Bill, or it will be ineffective if passed, without reference to the proper committee of the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Bill does not 'propose to alienate any part of the public domain.

Yes, it does. It gives authority in dozens of clauses to do exactly what is proposed here. It confers authority on the Governor in Council to alienate portions of the pubic domain ; so does this resolution of my hon. friend.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, The point I make is this, that the public domain is held to be a part of the public revenue, and that any proposal to alienate any part of the public domain should be treated as a money Bill.

I do not know whether it would have any influence on your judgment, Mr. Speaker, to know that a resolution practically to this effect was moved by the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Wilbert McIntyre), while the Bill was in committee, and was put to the vote of the committee. That resolution was for the Governor in Council to
Set apart and provide lands to be sold for the purpose of maintaining a fund to be used for the encouragement of higher education in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Was that
passed ?
ill-. R. L. BORDEN. No, but it was regarded as in order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Of course, I cannot very well take that as a precedent. I am merely calling attention to what seems to me to be no objection to a part of the resolution. My view may be wrong but it is that the last clause of the proposed amendment is clearly out of order.

I would ask your ruling, Mr. Speaker, as to whether or not the Bill itself which appropriates what the Prime Minister has described as public revenue and authorizes the Governor in Council to absolutely dispose thereof-whether the Bill can properly be read the third time and passed without complying with the rule in the British (North America Act which the first minister has invoked.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should think the same ruling would apply. If there is authority for the appropriation of public lands in the Bill itself, the same rule would apply.

There can be no doubt about that. There are at least a dozen sections which do that. Lgt me refer you, Sir, to sections 8 14 regarding the disposal of lands, to section 16 and the following regarding homestead patents, to section 32 where the Governor in Council is authorized to an unlimited extent to dispose of Dominion lands in the western provinces, and section 33 to the same effect. It is not necessary to enumerate them all. The Bill is full of them.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would suggest that as this is a matter of considerable importance, possibly the better way would be to postpone further consideration of the Bill until Monday next. In the meantime the matter can be looked into and further discussion be had if necessary.
On motion of Mr. Lake the debate was adjourned.

House in committee on Bill (No. 194) to amend the Customs Act.-(Mr. Paterson).
On section 2,-duty on equipment and repairs of coasting vessels.

I beg to move that the following be inserted instead of subsection 3 :
If, however, the owner or master of such vessel shall furnish good and sufficient evidence that the vessel, while in the regular course of her voyage, was compelled by stress of weather or casualty to put into a foreign port to maike the said repairs in order to secure the safety of the vessel or enable her

to reach her port of destination, or that it would be impracticable to make the repairs in Canada for the want of a dock of sufficient capacity to receive the vessel, it shall be competent for the Minister of Customs to authorize a refund of the duty on such repairs and such vessel shall not be liable to forfeiture. Provided that the repairs in the course of being made to the vesel in that foreign country, at the time when this Act comes into force or made prior to such time, shall not be dutiable under the said Act.

That would seem to cover what is reasonable. The only point that might arise is that, although there might be a dock of sufficient capacity, it might be engaged at the time. There might be another dock, but it would be at such a distance that it would be wrong to make the vessel take the voyage to reach it. Is that covered here, or is that within the discretion of the department ?
No. Since this Bill was introduced I have met a large deputation representing the shipping interests. But I was not able to depart from the principle of the Bill, which I think is right.
I think the principle is right.

But those suggestions they made I think are only fair. I think the effect of this Bill will be to promote the construction of more docks and ship building yards on the upper lakes. That is our expectation, but in the meantime, until we have those docks, we put in this Bill that a vessel is not liable unless the dock is sufficiently large to take her in. Capitalists who are meditating the construction of another dock, will thereby be inclined to construct it of sufficient length in which to make repairs on all vessels navigating the lakes.

If the minister wishes to act in strict accordance with the wording of his amendment, he could rule out any vessel, under certain circumstances, on which it would be impracticable to make repairs in Canada for the want of a dock of sufficient capacity. Now suppose that in Montreal, St. John or Halifax a dock Is of sufficient capacity to make repairs on that vessel, but during a week or a fortnight the dock is in use. Now it seems to me that the minister would not be allowed under that section to let that vessel off. There is' a dock of sufficient capacity to make repairs in Canada, but it is in use.
1 do not want to let her off under those circumstances.

Does the minister think it is fair ? Here is a vessel that comes in for repairs. The object is to get as much work as we can for Canadian docks. If we are going to embark on a system of encouraging ithe building of docks, we want
our vessels to make their repairs in those docks. Now a vessel comes in, there is a dock of sufficient size, but it is impossible for her to take that dock because it is filled, and it may be for a month or two.

Yes, that may occur to any vessel that wished to dock now. But she must wait her turn. If the captain does not want to wait his turn, it would be for him to consider whether it would be better for him to go to a foreign dock and to pay the duty involved. Supposing a vessel comes to one of our present docks and finds it engaged for ten days or two weeks, it will then be for the vessel to decide whether she will wait that time or go to a foreign country for repairs.
Yes, but the dock might be taken up for three months, and then the vessel owner might say, I am willing to get my repairs done here in Canada, but I cannot find a dock which will take me in.
But this covers the case where a man could not get it done if he waited a year. The case the hon. gentleman suggests is one in which delay might occur.

Would the minister tell me just now what are the regulations with reference to the coasting trade in Canada ? Have we reciprocal coasting trade privileges with other countries which grant the same to us ?

We have by virtue of an old order in council passed many years ago power to grant reciprocal coasting privileges with foreign countries, with Norway among others. We have that power now, but it ceases after the 1st of January next.
It ceases with all foreign countries ?
Yes.

Then, that seems to make section 2 even a little more harsh. Have we too many or too few vessels engaged in our coasting trade ? Is it not the object of every country, and should it not be particularly the object of Canada, to have as many vessels as possible interested in our coasting trade ? To come in, they have to be registered here, as I understand. That is, they cannot engage in the coasting trade without being registered in Canada.
That is right.
They become, to all intents and purposes, Canadian vessels and so build up our Canadian marine ?
Yes.

Is it of greater moment to get the vessels for our carrying trade or to get the little that comes from repairing the vessels ? It seems to me you run the risk

of discouraging what Canada wants to encourage in these days, because I do not think we have too much of a marine for the purpose of transporting our own product, and to bring in what we require. Does not the minister think it would have sonfe effect of that kind ? I think that if a Canadian vessel went into a foreign port and had the privilege of coasting in that foreign country but that a similar law to this were in force the Canadian owner would think it harsh that he could get no docking elsewhere to have his vessel put in a condition to carry on a coasting trade properly. Is it not better to have a staunch vessel come here and register and go into the trade of carrying our products rather than to have one that is not in such good repair ? Is it reasonable to keep a vessel for three or four months out of repair because she cannot get the privileges of docking ? I do not think it would be a good commentary upon our public methods if a vessel came in a couple of weens before the opening of the carrying season and found it impossible to get docking privileges for three months, being confronted with the alternative of waiting or going to a foreign port-which is some distance from us as we are situated-and on returning paying a fine, or duties equivalent to it-for having herself made staunch and seaworthy ?

But does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Poster) bear this in mind : There is absolute protection to the Canadian vessels ? (We talk of Canadian register and British register, but they are all British vessels). We do not allow any vessel to come in competition with vessels registering in Canada.
That is, in our coasting trade.

Yes. And, that being the case, is it unreasonable that the owner of the vessel so protected should be required to pay a duty of 25 per cent if he chooses to have repairs to his vessel made in a foreign country which accords us no such privileges, but charges 50 per cent on one of our Canadian vessels going there ?

But that is not exactly the choice in practice. The telegraph is everywhere nowadays, and the owner of the vessel learns before she starts exactly the circumstances that will face him if his vessel comes to Canada. He will say : I cannot send my vessel there to wait three months to be docked. Though a vessel engages in Canadian trade under Canadian register, you compel the owner, if he wants to make his vessel seaworthy, to pay a fine, even though you cannot offer him a chance to get the work done in this country.

But will you be able to give him a chance unless you take a Mr. FOSTER
step of this kind ? Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) put his money into a dry dock, under existing conditions ?

What I say is that there should be some available chance for the owner, within a reasonable time to get his repairs made. But, if it turns out that, for a whole season, he could not get docking privileges, lie has only the alternative of having his vessel hung up or being fined.
He would have to pay 25 per cent duty. Our whole tariff is on that line.
And all this time the grain and other produce of the country are waiting for vessels to transport them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Touching on the larger question of passing an order in council excluding foreign vessels from our coasting trade, I have this day put on the order paper a notice having in view an amendment of our coasting laws to enable us to modify the rules in such exceptional cases as may arise. The idea is to keep the coasting trade for our vessels as far as possible, but if there-are lines of trade where Canadian vessels are not available, and foreign vessels are ready to engage in the work, we may make a modification of the general rule. I mention that because it has a proper application to what the Minister of Customs says, and the subject will come up for discussion in a day or two.
What regulations have been made for our own vessels in our coasting trade ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The general action of the government would prevent foreign vessels taking part in our coasting trade after January 1st next. But it is proposed to give the Governor in council power to modify that in exceptional circumstances. It is represented, for instance, that there are large foreign vessels engaged in the coal trade which could not be duplicated at once, and there are no British vessels of the same class and character. Until these can be provided, it might be desirable to permit foreign vessels of a certain class to be temporarily employed in that service, and we are taking power under the law to make that modification. It is to give elasticity and meet the difficulty the hon. member for North Toronto has mentioned that we are asking parliament to give us the power to modify the regulations.

Has the minister been made acquainted with the fact that an agitation is going on among the owners of the sailing vessels of the maritime provinces with reference to the manner in which they have been treated at the mines ? This matter was up for discussion before. I know that some members of the House

made remarks indicating that the grievance would be remedied and that conferences were held with the coal companies with a view to having proper treatment extended to the sailing vessels. But I understand that the case is worse than it was last year. I would ask the minister if he is going to make a modification of the rule that he should include in the order in council regulations which would give equal rights to British shipping on the Atlantic coast everywhere where coal is shipped by sailing vessels. Each vessel should be loaded in its turn. It is nothing but right and just to our own wooden schooners and sailing vessels that that should be done. A feeling exists among the owners of sailing vessels that they are suffering an injustice under present conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The question to which the hon. gentleman from Prince Edward Island (Mr. A. A. McLean) has referred is certainly an important one, but it is entirely apart from the present discussion. It is not a question between British vessels and foreign vessels; it is a question between sailing vessels and steamers, which steamers may or may not be foreign or British. It is the tendency of the coal companies to give priority to steamers, not necessarily foreign steamers, and to keep sailing vessels waiting. So that, the question of foreign vessels does not enter into it. However, it is certainly a very important question. I understood some months ago that there was a good deal of complaint and I was under the impression that the coal companies had met the difficulty themselves in some degree. I have not of late had the matter brought to my notice. It is not a question that is, easy to deal with. At all events it is not a question between British vessels, or Canadian vessels and Norwegian vessels; it is a question between sailing vessels and steamers; so that it does not affect the question of dealing with foreign countries.
How does this new regulation compare with the regulation in the United States with regard to repairs ?
They charge double what we charge. They charge 50 per cent and we charge 25.
It is on the same lines.

Yes. I may say with reference to the Bill to which my hon. friend * has referred, lest it might create some misapprehension, some uneasiness, or lead to expectations that will not be gratified that this Bill will have reference to exceptional circumstances which I do not anticipate will occur on the great lakes. Therefore, I want it to be understood that if the Bill receives the sanction of the House and the exceptional circumstances take place, parties who have boats on the lakes will not be expecting that there will be help given them there.
Their competitors are, of course, our American competitors who guard quite as jealously as we do their coasting trade, and I think our shipowners on the lakes would object to relaxing, except under very exceptional circumstances, the coasting laws that we maintain. What the hon. gentleman refers to would be the possibility of exceptional circumstances arising on the Atlantic coast.
Relating more to Norwegian vessels ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They having entered into our coal trade to a considerable extent and some time being required to bring about new conditions.
In order to set a good example to others and, having given a good deal of consideration to this measure, I think we need not say anything more about it.	[DOT]

I would like to ask the minister if this clause covers a case where a vessel bound for a port. This seems to say that a vessel being compelled by stress of weather, or by a casualty, to make repairs, the minister may remit the duty when she arrives in Canada. But, suppose she is bound for a port. Suppose that in place of being driven into the port of New York she is bound for New York, something happens on the way and it is necessary that repairs should be made, does the clause cover a case of that kind ?
I think so. We will have to be the judges of that.

Before you report the Bill, Mr. Chairman, there is a matter that I have some interest in and which is of interest to the particular part of the country from which I come. It has reference to item 447 of the tariff. It may appear to be a small matter but it seems to be very far reaching.
I give notice that I am going to bring up the woollen schedule.

The item reads :
447. Portable engines with boilers, in combination, horse-powers and traction engines, for farm purposes, wind stackers and threshing machine separators, including baggers, weighers and self-feeders therefor, and finished parts thereof for repairs.
The department take the position that the repairs provided for here only apply to those items in this section after the semi-colon.
I do not think this is in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. gentleman is out of order. I do not think that point is mentioned in this Bill.
It Is not.
I want to move an amendment to this Bill to have it provided for.
You cannot do it on this Bill.
Provided however
We have had a ruling which my hon. friend must have heard. Has the member who is on his feet obtained the assent of the Governor General to this matter ?
It is a matter which interests our western people very much.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is out of order.
The interpretation is entirely different and far from what we believed we were getting when this item went through.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Bring it up on going into Supply.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 133) to amend the Boards of Trade Act. He said : Mr. Speaker, this is a Bill from the Senate to amend the general Act respecting the organization of boards of trade. There is a provision in what is known as the Boards of Trade Act, chap. 124 of the revised statutes, as to the organization of boards of trade by filing certificates of the proceedings with the Secretary of State. The existing law contemplates that there shall be a board of trade for a district which is set apart. A case has arisen at Battle-ford. There is already a board of trade in the town of Battleford and it is desired to organize one in the town of North Battle-ford.
Five miles away.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
lit is not very far away; it is separated from Battleford by the river and there are two communities. North Battleford desires to have a board of trade and it is found that there is not the power to organize another board of trade because it is within the district which has been assigned to another board, and the object is to so amend the Act that under conditions of that character an independent board may be organized.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 2,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I move to amend that section so as to make it read:	' But shall

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: continue to be subject to any liability standing upon the books of that board against them.'
Is it a feature of the Board of Trade Act that a person shall not be a member of more than one board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is assumed that where a board is already in existence they may not wish to have another board created, and if one wishes to withdraw he may be free to do so, but that shall not relieve him of any obligation which exists.

Does this Bill not go further; does it not say when the certificate is recorded members of the board in the existing district who reside in another district shall cease to be members? You might have a member of the old board who would be a most important and useful man on the new board.
Mr. MeCRANEY. That provision is made because there are judicial functions possessed by the board of trade and it is desired that there should not be any conflict of these functions over the same territory. The point that a member of the new board shall cease to be a member of the old can be very easily gotten over by his being reelected and reinstated.
Would it not be a simple matter in connection with Battleford and North Battleford to issue a charter to the old board and a charter to the new board and divide their territory by the river?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is the effect of the Bill.
Mr. MeCRANEY. I had that matter up before the Deputy Minister of Justice and he found there was no power in the Boards of Trade Act to restrict either as to their judicial functions or as to the territory, nor could the board of trade of its own motion restrict the territory over which it had jurisdiction. There is no authority in the Boards of Trade Act for the Governor in Council or any person here to do that. We endeavoured to get this matter through by obtaining the consent of the existing board of trade to a limitation of their territory, and I have a resolution to that end, but it was found ineffective by the Department of Justice. Then the proposition was made that the existing corporations should be dissolved and that two new charters should be granted concurrently but the deputy minister pointed out that apparently there was no provision in this Act for the dissolution of any existing board of trade although almost every other corporation is provided for.
Then why not amend the Boards of Trade Act without cutting it up like this?

You say that when the certificate is recorded members of the board of the existing district who reside in the-new district shall cease to be members of the old board. By what right do we legislate here that a man living in North Battle-ford shall not retain, if he wishes, his membership In the board of trade in which he has been initiated long before, where he has his affiliations and his interests. Why should you say he shall cease to belong to that board of trade?
Suppose he resides in North Battleford and has his business in South Battleford.
Yes; North Battleford may be some of these days a great residential suburb and it might want its residents to be members of the board of trade of old Battleford.

The point mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) comes up exactly in the case of Mr: Prince who has stores in both places and who is an influential member of both boards of trade. Should _we ever have rival towns and rival interests it is desirable there should be men who would be members of both boards.
And this legislation would render that impossible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It seems to assume that they should be members of the board of trade in the district in which they reside.
Why not just hold them liable for any liability standing on the books of the board ?

I might point out to the Minister of Finance that all over the province of Ontario-and 1 presume the same thing exists in the province of Quebec -some members of boards of trade in the country towns and smaller cities are also members of the board of trade of Toronto or of Montreal. It is not wrong for a man to be a member of both boards.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it is desirable for men to be members of both boards : it prevents local rivalry. I will ask that this section be allowed to stand in order that the point may be considered by the Department of Justice.
Section 2 allowed to stand.
On section 3, procedure to change boundaries of districts.
The district of a board of trade is not necessarily coterminus with the boundaries of the town ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Is it sufficiently guarded ?
A board of trade might make application to enlarge its territory so as to encroach on the territory of another board of trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
You would have to trust to the Governor in Council.
On section 4, dissolution of corporation.
How is it to be made to appear to the Governor in Council that a board has ceased to exercise its franchise?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That appears in a great many Acts. Whenever representations are made that will satisfy lie Governor in Council of a given condition of affairs.
Is there not a legal process by which any board of trade can dissolve itself ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It appears not.

Bill (No. 130) to amend the Naturalization Act-Sir Wilfrid Laurier-read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
What is the present enactment ?'

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The present clause is that in the province of Manitoba the presentation of the certificate which is requisite may be made either in the county court having jurisdiction where the aliens reside, or if there is no county court having jurisdiction there, then to the couuty eourt of the 'county nearest to his residence, or to the county court, the place of holding which is nearest to his residence. The purpose of the change is to confer concurrent jurisdiction in the matter of naturalizing on the Court of King's Bench, and to provide that the application for naturalization may be made either to the Court of King's Bench during its sittings in the district within which the alien resides, or to a judge of the Court of King's Bench sitting in court in the judicial district within which the alien resides, or to the county court. The repetition of the phrase, ' in the judicial district within which the alien resides,' in the ninth and tenth lines of the clause seems to make the provision ridiculous, and those words ought to be omitted. I move to strike them out. The effect of striking them out will be simply this, that the application for naturalization in Manitoba may be made either in the county court as at present or to the Court of King's Bench at the ordinary sittings when the judge goes to hold court in any particular district, or to a judge sitting in court, which will mean any ordinary sitting in Winnipeg, or, if there should happen to

be an extra sitting in tbe county where the alien resides, there will be the privilege of naturalizing at such extra sitting.
Does the Minister of Justice not think it would be necessary to have the naturalization done where the alien resides ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The application may be presented to a judge wherever he holds court.
Provided he is holding court where the alien lives.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Anywhere in the province where he is holding court.

That is likely to lead to considerable abuse. Sometimes naturalization papers are taken very wrongfully. Suppose that from the outskirts of the province some papers are sent into the court in Winnipeg, away from where any one acquainted with him would have an opportunity to contest. It would be better to have the application made to any court sitting within the judicial district.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The application for naturalization has to be made to the officials of the court in the locality where the applicant resides. The applicant has to satisfy those local officials that he has complied with the requirements of the Act. He does that by affidavit and all the formalities the Act requires. Then the clerk gives him a certificate that the Act has been complied with, and the applicant may present that certificate to a judge in Winnipeg sitting in court or to a judge in the locality where he resides.

In the province of Ontario the usual method was for the application to be taken before a magistrate and then sent to the county court, but without any change in the law, an order was sent to the various Crown attorneys-certainly to the Crown attorney in the district I represent-not to accept any longer affidavits of that kind and requiring the applicant to appear in person before the Crown attorney and there register in person. That has proved a great hardship in the case of a number of men who wanted to become naturalized, but did not want to take up the time to travel to a county town and appear in person before the Crown attorney.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This legislation has no application to the province of Ontario whatever.

When the hon. minister speaks of local officials does that mean only the county crown attorney or some other official ?
Mr. 'AYLESWORTH. Of course, the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Wm. Wright) is speaking of the practice in Ontario. In Mr. AYLESWORTH.
that province it is the clerk of the county court in each county. I do not know whether there are any other officials who have the right to pass upon these questions, but I know, in practice, that they always go to the clerk of the county court.
I can tell the hon. minister that his department sends out letters of instructions to the county Crown attorney, which I have read, ordering him to issue these certificates, and he only to do it.

The hon. member (Mr. Wm. Wright) is technically correct. I have had to sign many of these in my capacity of clerk of the peace. There are two courts in Ontario at which aliens may be naturalized. One is the general sessions of the peace, in which the certificate is signed bv the clerk of the peace, who is usually tlie county Crown attorney-who is clerk of that court. There is also the assize court, where they are signed by the local registrar as clerk of that court. The Minister of Justice reminds me that they are ordinarily signed by the clerk of the county court, but he signs in his capacity as local registrar of the high court.
1 understood the member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) to say that there are no county courts in Manitoba-
I said there were no such things as counties. We have county courts.

In only one of these cases must the officer be a resident of the county in which the alien resides, and that is a justice of the peace. And so the alien might make the oath before a person two hundred miles away from where he resides.
The stipendiary magistrate would have to be a resident of the district.
Not necessarily.

I can hardly imagine a I stipendiary magistrate acting outside his

district. In fact, that would be contrary to the fundamental principles of the magistracy. If my hon. friend will be fair, I say that a stipendiary magistrate would have to reside in the district.
The magistrate might not live in the district where the alien is.

But he would have to be within his own district. So far as a notary public is concerned, I know that in New Brunswick he is appointed for the province, and so he might administer the oath anywhere in the province. But the point is that it is necessary to get the certificate of some official stating that he knows the facts, and that the alien has complied with the requirements of the law as to residence or service and is entitled to naturalization. This certificate must then be taken to the court and posted for three weeks in the office of the clerk. At the meeting of the court the papers are taken and read, as a rule, the first day of the court. They remain till the last day, when formal application is made by the clerk or by some attorney interested, and, if no objections are raised, the order issues!
And a record is kept?

The record is made by the court. In New Brunswick there are two courts to which application may be made. The first is the county court, in which the record is made by the clerk of the court. The other is the circuit court or nisi prius of the Supreme Court, where the record is made by the clerk of the circuit Either has power to sign the certificate! This is handed to the alien, and he is then a naturalized British subject.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Carveil) seems pretty well posted, and I would like to ask him a question. There is a misapprehension-or let us say an apprehension-in the minds of many throughout Canada that by joining the militia an alien becomes a British subject.
No.

I am well aware that it is not the case, but there is that belief. In some countries it is true that the moment a man becomes a regular soldier of that country he becomes a subject. Now, will the hon. gentleman please explain the matter?

In order that a person may become naturalized in Canada he must have resided in Canada for three years, or have been in the service of the Dominion of Canada, or some province of the Dominion in a foreign country for three years -his service or residence, or both, must make up three years. Then he makes
oath, as I have already said, and then goes to the proper court in the province as provided by the law. In Ontario he goes to the general sessions of the peace of the county in which he resides, or to the court of assize and nisi prius during sittings in the county ; in Quebec, to any circuit court within the territorial limits of the jurisdiction of which he resides ; in Nova Scotia, to the Supreme Court during the Sittings in the county in which he resides or to tlie county court ; in New Brunswick, to the Supreme Court during the sittings in the county in which he resides or to the circuit court in the county, or to the county court ; in British Columbia, to the Supreme Court of British Columbia sitting in the electoral district in which he resides, or to the court of assize, or to the county court ; in Manitoba, he may only go to the county court. I will read the section, so that there may be no question. It is subsection (f>
of section 16 :
.	Manitoba, to the county court having
jurisdiction where the alien resides, or if there is no county court having jurisdiction there, then to the county court of the county nearest to his residence, or the county court the place of holding which, is nearest to his residence.
The object of this Bill is to provide a little more machinery and to majie it a little easier, perhaps, to become naturalized.

Does not the hon. gentleman think that the object is to keep the signing power as closely as possible to the place in which the alien lives ? This whole difficulty has arisen because the Minister of Justice is bringing in a Bill which does not violate this general principle, but proposes to say in Manitoba what does violate tlie general principle. We should hold to tlie old principle of keeping the last power which signs as closely as possible to the first power which puts into operation what shall make a citizen.

speechtext:

In Manitoba, to the Court of King's Bench during its sittings in the judicial district in which the alien resides.
Everybody knows what that is, that is when the judge goes to try causes in the Superior Court in the particular district in which the alien resides, twice in the year in Ontario and twice in the year, I suppose, in Manitoba, what we call the assizes.' Then it is repeated again in the next line.

Before a judge of the Court of King's Bench sitting in the judicial district in which the alien resides.
On section 2,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Three amendments have been suggested to me by the clerk of the peace in the city of Toronto, and which will affect Ontario. The first is that the document to be presented to the court shall be, not as now the certificate only, but the certificate accompanied by the oaths of residence and allegiance. So these papers would be filed in the court which grants the naturalization, along with the certificate.
All over Canada ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That would apply to the whole Dominion. Under the law as it now stands the applicant for naturalization presents nothing but the certificate that he has taken the oath. The clerk of the peace at Toronto suggests that these oaths are important documents, and that they ought to accompany the certificate, and be filed with the certificate in the court from which the order of naturalization issues. That will be accomplished by adding to the word ' certificate ' the following words :
And oaths of residence and allegiance or service and allegiance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is another amendment proposed to section 19 of the Act. It is as to the day on which this certificate should be presented at the court. Under the present law, by section 19, the presentation of such certificate has to be made in open court on the first day of some general sittings of the court, and then, at the conclusion of the court the order of naturalization issues. It is proposed that it should be changed so as to read that the certificate should be presented in open court and on the first day of some general sittings of the court, or one of the first four days of the sittings and that the court on the last day of the sittings, or on the fifth day, when the sittings shall last more than four days, shall direct that the certificate of the applicant shall be filed of record in the court. The effect would be to allow the certificate to be presented on any of the first four days of the sittings instead of on the first day only.

This seems to be rather a dangerous provision. One of the objects of presenting the certificate to the clerk of the court on the first day of the sittings is that it shall remain open to inspection during the sittings and anybody can object. If you are going to have a session of the court running as far as five days and if it is to be allowed to put the certificate on file on the fourth day you are going to give no opportunity to anybody to object.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Suppose the coui't does not last more than two days ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Quite necessarily, if the certificate were not presented on the first day of the sittings, the length of the period of objection would be diminished.
It might be three, it might be four, or it might be two days, but see what you have as it stands at present. If the court only lasts half an hour it is all over in half an hour. If the court lasts two weeks you have possibly four days less in which to object. If it lasts five days you might have only one day.

That is not an answer to the objection I make. If, as the law stands, a party is watching the names of the people who are proposed for naturalization, he goes on the first day. If there are none filed that day his duty is over. Under the change he would have to go every day.

Further than that, the notice of the application must be posted up in the office of the court for three weeks prior to the sitting of the court. Everybody has noticed that so many persons are applying for naturalization and there are those who may be desirous of opposing these applications. Under the Act as it stands I can go there to oppose that application on a certain day, I probably travel 50 or 100 miles in order to go to the county town and it may happen that those who are anxious to get them through willy nilly may wait until the fifth day and then during the half hour that I am away present their applications and deprive me of the opportunity of offering any opposition. There surely is no hardship in making one day certain and that the first day of the sittings of the court upon which these applications shall be filed notice of which shall be required to be posted three weeks in advance.

I do not think the minister is wedded to this particularly but there seems to be a misunderstanding as to the object. As the hon. member for West Algoma has pointed out, three weeks notice is given prior to the sitting of the court that such and such persons will make application at that court.
Mr. SAM- HUGHES. At that court or any other court ?

It must be at the next court. I do not see how any hardship can be imposed upon anybody, because, instead of going on the first day you will not have to go until the fourth day. Of course, there is always the possibility that the court will have got through with its business and will have adjourned. As a matter of fact in cases like these, there is always somebody at the court who is watching and who, if necessary, will remain at the court. The only object I can see on the part of the gentleman from Toronto who made that

proposition is to provide against the possibility of a person, not being present on the first day, being excluded.
They must give notice beforehand and he must be ready. The only question is whether everybody has to keep watching for four or five days.
I admit there are two sides to the question and I do not think that the minister is very anxious to press it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I made the proposal simply because the clerk of the court at Toronto, a gentleman of considerable experience in these matters, thought that it would be an improvement on the present law. I set no particular store on it one way or the other and if hon. gentlemen think we had better make no change 1 am quite content.
Amendment withdrawn.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is one further change that is possibly of practical importance, to the officials, at least. Section 47 of the present Act prescribes the fee which the clerk of the court is entitled to receive for his work. It shall be the sum of twenty-five cents and no more. It is worded in this way :	For his services the
clerk of the court shall
Be entitled to receive from the person naturalized the sum of 25 cents and no more; and no further or other fee shall be payable for or in respect of such certificate.
I am told that in some of the provinces the clerks of the court are paid by the provincial governments a salary for their services in connection with such matters. I do not know that that would occur to anybody to be a contravention of this section, but in others of the provinces clerks are not paid by salary. They are paid by fees with respect to each piece of work they do. That is the case in the province of Ontario where the clerk of the county court, or the clerk of the peace, receives so much for preparing each order of the court, so much for each piece of work lie does, not being paid a salary, but being paid in proportion to the amount of work he does. What this gentleman in Toronto says is that for years past, long before he took the office, these fees were paid by the government without question or objection. It has now been questioned whether or not he is entitled to anything more than the 25 cents in respect of each one of these cases. He brought the matter before me asking an official interpretation of the statute and I declined to express any Opinion about it, thinking it was not any part of my duty. He then asked that the matter be made clear. Let me point out just how it stands so that it may be seen whether there is at present any obscurity and whether that 380
obscurity if it exists ought not be cleared off :
The clerk shall be entitled to receive for the certificate from the person naturalized the sum of 25 cents and.no more and no further or other fee shall be payable for or in respect of such certificate.

And no further or other fee shall be payable by the person naturalized for or in respect of such certificate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I was Under the impression, which has been confirmed by the hon. member (Mr. Turriff), that in each judicial district in the new provinces there was a local clerk of the Supreme Court. In the province of Quebec, with the clerk of the circuit court of the circuit within which such person resides.
