WThat is the intention with regard to this vote ? What particular wharfs do you propose to build ?

This is for the purpose of paying the provincial government one-half the cost of certain wharfs which they have either constructed or will construct during the present year. I would suppose however that these probably have been, built and the claim would be pending by the province against this government because I see this is a revote. Some fifteen years ago there was an understanding w-ith the provincial government that the latter would construct certain wharfs upon the St. John river and tributaries. As regards the location, this government has not interfered. All that was stipulated was that the plans and specifications should be first submitted to the engineer of the Department of Public Works. Then, when the wharf

was completed to the satisfaction of the government engineer, this government paid one half the cost of construction. I would assume that this would be a claim for some wharfs built last year because this is a revote.

The hon. minister would have some knowledge because this time last year he was a member of the local administration. I understand there is a large amount unpaid. Evidently nothing was paid last year. I understand that an amount equal to, if not exceeding this vote, is still outstanding against the federal government for its half share of these wharfs already constructed.	.

I am inclined to think not. My attention was called to the matter just before the close of the last fiscal year. The then Commissioner of Public Works from New Brunswick was urging the payment. He was asked to send in the details. I remember seeing the Bill and it included some wharfs built in other sections of the province. He was informed that, under this vote, that amount could not be paid. All that would be paid would be the wharfs on the River St. John and tributaries. I wrote him to send the necessary details to the department and the money would be paid. Whether the details have been furnished or not I cannot say.
"Would it be in your department ?
Yes.
Have none been sent ?
Not by communicatiou with me.
Or your department.
I am not aware. It might or might not come to my notice, but I would suppose that the provincial government would communicate directly with me.
Does the minister say that a claim would be made against the Public Works Department and not be brought to his attention ?

A claim might be addressed to the engineer of my department. In the ordinary course it would come to me provided anything in it required special attention. But if everything was in proper form, it would go through the engineer's department and be paid by the accountant in the ordinary way without reference to me.
It seems strange that a claim from the province of New Brunswick against the federal government would not go to the minister and would be paid without his knowing anything about it.
That might be.
A matter amounting to $4,000 or $5,000.

Yes, it is voted by parliament, and then, in the ordinary way, upon the receipt of all the vouchers and necessary certificates it would be paid without coming to me. I will find out if it has been paid. The matter has not been pressed by the new government, I believe, at all.
No communication has been received?
The chief engineer tells me, none. .

The other evening the minister and I had some discussion of a matter that is of great importance to the province of New Brunswick generally and especially to the constituency I have the honour to represent, as some of the lower reaches of the St. John river pass through the county of Kings. On that subject I .would like to know the hon. gentleman's intentions with regard to the future. The hon. gentleman made two or three state-* ments, and, as these seemed to be at variance with each other, it was difficult for me to know on which he intended to rely.
I understood him to say that it was the intention of the federal government to mete out the same treatment to the province of New Brunswick as to the other provinces having navigable rivers such as the St. John, with reference to wharfs and works of that character, and that those required would be built at the entire cost of the government. In a later speech, as I understood him, he put forward the idea that the province would still be required to pay its share of half the cost of wharfs except in the case perhaps of one or two which would be built at the cost of the federal government.
I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) on reflection will not say that I made reference to one or two wharfs which this government would build.
What is the minister's intention with regard to these? It is a matter of importance, and not one to be treated lightly.

When these items were last before the committee I referred to the fact that for many years the provincial government had been building wharfs on the St. John river and its tributaries, as well as in other sections of the province. I said that fifteen years or more ago the federal government, on request which was made to the then Minister of Finance, agreed to make contributions for a few wharfs to the extent of one-half. I said also that in later years that policy had been extended and more wharfs constructed.

Will the hon. gentleman undertake to say that the government that

preceded this one did not pay the same proportion of cost of wharfs that were erected?	.
1 said they paid half, but not all of the wharfs.
My understanding was exactly the contrary.

I was a member of the provincial government and I know *that many wharfs were built by that government to which the forpaer federal government did not contribute, but the federal government did contribute to a few. In later years, after Mr. Blair became minister, the policy was extended and larger contributions were made. The hon. gentleman has only to take up the vote for the St. John fiver and he will find that in recent years the amounts paid were considerably in excess of those paid down to 1895. I stated that my opinion had been that It was pro' per for the federal government, to a reasonable extent, and with due justice to every section of the Dominion, to undertake the construction of wharfs wholly at its own expense. I said, at the same time, that I thought it would be very regettable If the provincial government should cease building wharfs to which this government might contribute one-half, because the result would be that the people would not in the near future receive the accommodation desirable. My hon. friend (Mr. Fowler)) speaks of our building wharfs on the St. Lawrence, the Saguenay, the great lakes and even the smaller lakes. That is true, but many sections of the upper provinces are crying out for wharf accommodation and have been for years, but have not been able to get it because the expenditure is limited by the government's resources. On many parts of the St. Lawrence and Saguenay wharfs have been built by private companies. If the hon. gentleman travels on these rivers he will find a large number of wharfs not built by this government. When the supplementary estimates come down I think the hon. gentleman will find that reasonable provision has been made for building a reasonable number of wharfs wholly at the expense of the federal government. Of course, the hon. gentleman would not expect me to indicate in advance what they are or what the amounts may be. My policy, so far as I can exercise my own views as a member of the government, will be to construct year after year a reasonable number of wharfs on the St. John river and Its tributaries wholly at the expense of the government. At the same time I hope that the policy of the provincial government of paying half the cost of construction will not be discontinued all at once or in the near future, because the hon. gentleman knows that by reason of the large number of steamers navigating the St. John, Grand lake, Washedemoak, Bel-lisle and the Kennebecasis, a great many Mr. FOWLER.
wharfs are required to give the proper accommodation. If the provincial government does not contribute even in a small way, some of the much needed accommodation for the people may not be given.

The hon. gentleman knows that I did not expect or a-k him to state what wharfs he intends to build at present; I asked him for a declaration of the policy he proposed to pursue. To compare the Saguenay with the St. John is, to my mind, an absurdity. He speaks of the people of the Saguenay crying out for more wharfs. They have cried to some purpose, for since 1901 they have had exepnded upon the Saguenay over $100,000 of the federal money.
Not in wharfs alone, but in dredging also-largely dredging.
No, wharfs. One wharf alone cost $40,000.
Will the hon. gentleman give me the name of it?
I have not the name at the moment, but I believe the cost of it was $41,000.
I think the hon. gentleman is in error.
I will get the name Of the wharf. My hon. friend from East Slm-eoe tells me that one wharf in the St. Lawrence below Quebec
We are speaking of the Saguenay.

Yes, and I will get the name of the wharf for the hon. gentleman. To compare those two rivers is absurd, one a great river with its tributaries penetrating the centre of the province of New Brunswick and the other a small branch of the St. Lawrence river.
Would the hon. gentleman give us the length of the Saguenay ?
It is considerably shorter than the St. John river, and considerably smaller. I doubt if my hon. friend knows the length of it.
I know It is upwards of a hundred miles in length.
The St. John is 400 miles.
The navigable portion of the Saguenay is 100 miles. My information is that vessels drawing 25 feet go up the Saguenay for a distance of 100 miles.
I do not think it is so, the hon. gentleman does not know of his own knowledge. *
My chief engineer tells me it is so, and he would know.

Compare the two rivers by reason of their importance, by reason of the amount of traffic carried on them-'that is the proper comparison, rrnere is not a tithe of the traffic carried on the Saguenay that there is on the St. John, and that is the true test of the importance of a river. A few steamers go up the Saguenay carrying tourists, but practically no business is transacted on it. But my hon. friend knows the tremendous volume of business transacted on the St. John river, and it is necessary to have these public works. Yet the province has been discriminated against, and for over a year you have not paid even the money that you agreed to pay.
Mr. PUG-SLEY. 1 must contradict my hon. friend with regard to that. The moment the necessary papers and certificates are presented to satisfy the Auditor General, that moment any claim the province of New Brunswick has will be paid.
It has not been paid, and the hon. gentleman admits it.
I take it for granted that the necessary certificates have not been presented.

It is a strange thing that the government of which the hon. gentleman is a member does not know enough to sign certificates. It is a reflection on his late colleagues. I am surprised that the hon. gentleman should make that statement, it is rather unkind to his late Commissioner of Public Works. I am sorry it is necessary for me to defend the late colleagues of the hon. gentleman against himself. Now with regard to this item, I am glad to hear the minister state that he proposes to build these wharfs out of the federal grant entirely. If the hon. gentleman recognizes the importance of the River St. John and the necessity of these works, it will not be necessary for tile provincial government to contribute. The provincial government of the province of Quebec does not contribute to public works of this character, and why should the government of the province of New Brunswick, which is very much poorer in financial resources than the great province of Quebec.

It seems to me the hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) is getting very anxious about wharfs along the River St. John, much more in fact than he has been in the past. I have been in this House four sessions, and I have not heard any great wail from the hon. member about wharfs on the river St. John until the present time. I think he is anxious to help out some of his friends in New Brunswick, or he would not be regaling the House tonight on the question of wharfs. We spent two hours one afternoon last week hearing the hon. gentleman lecture the Minister of Public AVorks in regard to these wharfs.
I can tell the hon. gentleman that the people of the province of New Brunswick realize who it is that is assisting them; they know why the hon. gentleman takes up the time of the House in finding fault with the Minister of Public Works, although the Minister of Public AVorks is going further than any other minister has ever gone towards assisting the building of wharfs on the river St. John, and is laying down a new principle which I think is correct, and which the hon. member for Kings and Albert will agree is correct. But he is not satisfied with that, he wants the Minister of Public Works to lay down the doctrine now that he will build ail the wharfs on the River St. John, and not ask the local government, not even allow tlie local government to do so if they wish. I think the hon. gentleman is unfair, he is showing too great an anxiety to asist his political friends in the province of New Brunswick. If he thinks he can make any capital out of it he is welcome to go on and repeat these things. But the people of New Brunswick are not children, they know what the hon. gentleman is talking about, and why he is talking.
Now there is another branch of this case that I want to refer to, although it more properly comes under the previous item that was taken up when I was not present, and that is the necessity of doing something towards improving navigation on the upper portion of the River St. John above tide water. We hear a great deal about building wharfs, and dredging and improving navigation from Fredericton to St. John. Years ago when the counti'y was first settled, it was possible for steamers drawing some five or six feet of water to ply to Woodstock, a distance of 65 miles above tide water, and at certain seasons of the year to Grand Falls, a distance of 75 miles above that. But of late years, since the country has been cleared up, the volume of water is greater in the spring of the year and less in summer. But we have always had a steamer from Fredericton to Woodstock, and that is the only means of communication with the outside world for some 60 odd miles which Is afforded to some of the best and oldest settled portions of the province. But this year that steamer has been taken off and I hope the minister will see his way clear to take some steps to' dredge the river, or by some aid to make it possible for a steamer to ply from Fredericton to Woodstock during a portion of the summer. I believe that the bars could be dredged out. There is plenty of water in nine-tenths of the stretch of this river, but there are a number of bars which are so high now in low water that navigation is impossible. I strongly urge the minister to place an amount in the estimates, this year if possible, in order that at least a survey may be made. Perhaps It is not possible to do anything in the way of dredging, but I think a survey could be made, and if a competent engineer decides

1200S
it is possible, then I think we have as good a right to ask the department to spend some of this money towards improving navigation above the city of Fredericton as we have below it.

I must congratulate the Minister of Public Works upon the wet nurse with which he has provided himself in the person of the hon. member for Oar-leton (Mr. Carvell). The hon. member for Carleton has seen fit to read me a lecture upon the manner in which I perform what I conceive to be my duty with regard to matters in connection with my own constituency. I would have the hon. member for Carleton to understand that when he makes the statement that he did make, that this was the first time that he had heard me make any ' wail,' as he called it, with regard to this wharf since the minister has made his declaration of policy, it is because the hou. gentleman was not attending to the duties of his office as a member of this House. If he had been properly attending to his duties he would have known that there has not been a session since he has been here, nor since I have been in the House during eight years, that I have not brought up this very matter, that I have not discussed this very matter at every session since 1900. I think that on every occasion when this estimate was under discussion I have asked that the policy of the government with regard to the province of New Brunswick be changed.
Well, I want to tell the hon. gentleman that if he states that this is the first time he has heard it, it is because the hou. gentleman does not attend very well to his duties and is not very often in the House. The hon. gentleman's hearing is acute enough. It is a strange thing that the minister had to have the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) come to his aid. Is this the reed upon which the hon. gentleman proposes to rest? He will find it a broken one. I do not think the hon. gentleman will further his own interests in having that hon. gentleman get up and attempt to read me a lecture as to what I shall do and as to what I shall not do. I asked the minister for a declaration of policy, because I do not understand what he proposes as a policy with regard to wharfs in New Brunswick. I had good reason for not understanding it from the fact that the minister, when he made a statement the other day, made two or three statements. One he made under the stress of temper. The minister very seldom loses his temper In the House, but on this particular occasion he did lose it.
I do not remember doing so.

It is singular the hon. gentleman did not remember, when it Is only ocasionally he does lose his temper.
Mr. CARVELL
He may have said things that he did not mean. I gave him credit for that, and I asked him to-night, in a very civil and proper manner, for a declaration of policy in regard to this matter. Simply because I attempted to do that, the hon. member for Carleton thought it was necessary to read me a lecture. I am surprised that the hon. member for Carleton should find it necessary to say anything in the House to-night. I read in the newspapers that the hon. member for Carleton and the would-be member for York
Will-be.
Would-be.
You said the 'would-be member for York ' ; coming events cast their shadow's before them.

The minister is only joking, and it is a very poor joke, too, because the minister knows that Mr. Whitehead has no chance of being the member for York as opposed to the hon. sitting member for York, Mr. Crocket. But we read in the newspapers supporting the administration that the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., and the Liberal candidate for York had waited on the minister In regard to this dredging and had got a pledge or promise from the minister that this was to be done. Then why does the hon. gentleman take up the time of the House to-night in making a plea that this work should be done? The hon. gentleman accuses me of wasting the time of the House, and here the hon. gentleman himself takes up the time of this committee in urging upon the minister something that the minister has already agreed to do. If that is not so, If the minister has not promised to do it, then the Liberal papers have stated in their columns that which is not a fact. Surely that cannot be possible. Surely the Liberal press would not do anything like that.
The minister does not think it.

The minister does not say anything. He will take it for granted that the Liberal newspapers are telling the truth, and I am surprised that the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., instead of expediting the passage of these estimates, is obstructing them. Let us see about this dredging. Before the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., had awakened to a sense of his duty in the premises, and before the Liberal candidate for York had waited upon the minister, the sitting member for York had taken this matter up in the House, had discussed it and had made a request of the minister. Not only that, but, as I understand it, certain gentlemen who were here from Fredericton had already waited upon the minister in regard to the importance of this work. So you see that it is

second thought on the part of the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., and the candidate for York.

It is quite true, as the hon. member for Kings and Albert has said, that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell), together with Mr. Whitehead, a very influential gentleman from Fredericton, had waited upon me with regard to the matter of improving the channel between Fredericton and Woodstock, and that they had also urged upon me the desirability of having a survey made at as early a date as possible.
I did not make the statement that it would be done, and I do not remember having seen anything in the newspapers that I did state it would be done, but I do remember telling these gentlemen that I trusted that I would be able to secure an appropriation for that purpose during the present session
That is the same thing.

I am strongly impressed with the great advantage which will result to that most important, most fertile and thoroughly well settled part of the country, if navigation between Fredericton and Woodstock could be so improved as to make it possible for steamers to navigate that river during the whole of the summer season. The people there for a considerable distance have no railway accommodation, and it would be of great benefit to them if they could have steamboat accommodation. While 1 cannot say to-night what will be done in regard to the matter, I will repeat the assurance which I gave to these gentlemen, that I am urging the matter upon the attention of my colleagues, and that I trust before this session closes, when the supplementary estimates are brought down, it will be found that such provision has been made for the purpose of making a survey during the present season as will be satisfactory to my hon. friend and to the people who are interested in this matter.
Just a word with regard to the remarks which the hon. member for Kings and Albert has made with reference to the St. John river as compared with the rivers in this section of 'the Dominion. While I appreciate to the fullest extent the importance of the St. John river and its tributaries, while I recognize the large amount of business that is done on these waters, I do not think that the interests of those of us who represent New Brunswick will gain anything by seeking to disparage the rivers which are in other sections of the Dominion, and my hon. friend, in seeking to belittle the river Saguenay-

I am not.
Mr. PUGSLEY-has shown a want of knowledge
The minister will pardon me.
The hon. gentleman will pardon me.
Will the hon. gentleman pardon me?
No, I will not pardon you ; time is too precious-lias shown a considerable) want of knowledge of the importance of the river Saguenay and the St. Lawrence.
You are not gaining anything by that course.

The river Saguenay is a river of about 100 miles in length, and I am sure that no matter how important Is the business done on the St. John, the business done on the Saguenay is not second, at all events, to that which is done on the St. John. Large steamers go up the river Saguenay, not only the ordinary passenger boats of the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company, but ocean steamers, vessels drawing 25 feet, go up as far as Chicoutimi, a distance of 100 miles from the mouth of the river. It is one of the most important rivers in Canada. The only reason why I referred to it was to emphasize the fact that there are many sections in this country, almost in every province, where the necessities of the public are very urgent in so far as wharf accommodation is concerned, and I only regret that I have not found it possible to comply with the very reasonable demands which have been made by members from all sections of Canada. The most we can do is to get along as weli as we can, and try to do the best we can to meet the various requirements of the country. That I propose to do so far as the province of New Brunswick and all the other provinces of the Dominion are concerned. With the means at my disposal I shall endeavour to give all reasonable accommodation to the various sections of the Dominion.

The Minister of Public Works with his usual unfairness has attempted to say that I was trying to belittle the Saguenay river. Does he think it is belittling the Saguenay river to say it does not compare in importance with the River St. John ? If the hon. gentleman carried that argument out to its logical conclusion he would think that I was belittling him were I to say that he would not measure up alongside some of the gentlemen who preceded him in his office. The hon. gentleman may be a big man and yet he may not be equal to some of the great men who preceded him as Minister of Public Works, and so the Saguenay may be a great river and yet not equal the great River St. John which Is amongst the most important of the inland waters of Canada and one of the greatest navigable rivers in the world. I do not think the hon. minister should be so unfair as to try to accuse me of belittling the Sague-

nay river. Nothing could be further from my thoughts than that, and I think the illustration I have given is one that must appeal to the hon. gentleman himself as being entirely to the point.
Having apologized to the Saguenay please go on with the business.

I did not need to apologize to tlie Saguenay, I only defended myself from the unfair attack the Minister of Public Works made on me.
St. Andrews harbour improvements, $10,000.

This is for the purpose of improving the harbour of St. Andrews at the mouth of Ste. Croix river. It is a good harbour in quite an important place and the channel needs to be straightened. We will continue the dredging work.
What did you spend last year ?
About $5,000. This may not all be devoted to dredging: we may use part of it for building a wharf.
Where are you dredging now ?

The western entrance.
St. John harbour-improvements, repairs and dredging, $400,000.

This is for the purpose of carrying on the work of improving the St. John harbour. It is intended to devote a portion of the vote to the building of the extension to the wharfs upon the northern side of the Sand Point slip. For the information of hon. gentlemen who are not familiar with St. John harbour I may say that for a number of years past work has been going on in the way of dredging and wharf building for the purpose of giving accommodation to the largest ocean steamers. That work was commenced about twelve years ago. It has been carried on very persistently since, and to-day St John harbour is very well equipped indeed with terminal facilities, but I think I may say these facilities are not sufficient even for the trade which now comes to the port, and they certainly will not be sufficient for the trade of the future because the trade of St. John is increasing year by year. The total exports from the port of St. John during the past winter reached the large sum of very nearly $25,000,000, and when hon. gentlemen consider that this enormous business has been achieved in the short time of about ten years they can see how rapidly St. John is fulfilling what I think to be its manifest destiny of becoming one of the great winter ports of Canada. When the city of St. John began this work the city of Portland in the State of Maine was Canada's winter port, at all events for the Mr. FOWLER
Height traffic. St. John started in at the expense of its own people to provide necessary facilities with a view of giving accommodation to ocean steamers. At first they undertook the work of dredging and wharf building at the expense of the citizens and upon the western side of the harbour upwards of $1,000,000 was expended by the city for this purpose. Two or three years ago, the Dominion government recognizing that St. John was doing a great national work ; doing a great Canadian work-because every one will recognize that any city which succeeds in doing what St. John succeeded in doing, namely, diverting the trade of Canada through Canadian channels is performing a national work-the Dominion government, as I say, recognizing that the city of St. John was doing a great work for Canada, in having demonstrated the fact that St. John could successfully compete with Portland for the winter trade of Canada, thought that it might fairly come to the assistance of St. John and undertake the work of carrying on further dredging operations. Not long ago a delegation came here from the city of St. John and they interviewed several members of the government and myself in regard to the government enlarging its obligations in this respeict and undertaking the building of wharfs on the western side of the harbour. As a result of the arguments which they impressed upon us I submitted the matter to council and was able to get them to agree to undertake at present the building of the further extension to the wharf upon the northern side of the Sand Point slip where the steamers of the Allan, Canadian Pacific Railway, and Donaldson lines come. A portion of this $400,000 will be devoted towards the building of this wharf. The remainder will be devoted partially to paying for dredging and partially to other work for the improvement of the harbour.

The historical sketch of the harbour of St. John given by the Minister of Public Works though fairly correct in the main, is not entirely accurate. He stated this work has been going on only for the last ten years, but I would remind him the work was commenced considerably before then. The first wharf built by the city in connection with these improvements was called the Connolly wharf, and that was built some years before 1895. The first winter port business was done in the winter of 1895. Since that time it has been increasing rapidly and it was only right and proper that the Dominion government should recognize its obligations to the city of St. John. Two or three years ago the government made a commencement in this connection and it has since continued its policy. As one of the representatives of the city of St. John I am very glad to see this sum in the estimates for carrying on that work. I would like the minister to state

what this $400,000 is supposed to do. Will any of this amount go to the oi'dinary repairs of the breakwater or is it for the purpose of building the wharf and doing what dredging is necessary. I would like to know what this amount is intended to complete.

This amount is intended to pay for the building of the wharf extension or so much of it as can be carried on during the present fiscal year. Out of this same vote will be paid the balance which is due for dredging, the finishing up of Mr. Mayes' contract which is called the old contract, the dredging out of the basin of Sand Point slip.
This will put the warehouses on the wharf ?

This will also put the warehouse which the government will build on the wharf. Then there is a certain work which is going on in connection with the repairs and maintenance of the breakwater and that will be paid out of this vote. There is some work at Fort Dufferin. It is not proposed at the present time to undertake the extension of the breakwater to Partridge island. There is considerable doubt as to the wisdom or necessity of making that extension. It will cost a very large sum of money, somewhere in the vicinity of $600,000 ; and while for some reasons it might be of advantage to have a breakwater because of the greater shelter it would afford from southwesterly storms, the chief engineer of my department, supported, I believe, by the city engineer of St. John, who has had large experience, believes it would have many disadvantages, among them the causing of an increased current in the harbour. I am inclined to think that a more desirable work is the dredging of the harbour below the Sand Point wharf, and building wharfs there so as to provide better accommodation.
The Sand Point wharf is the extreme wharf ?
Yes, the southerly point.

I am glad- that the minister has stated that the extension of the breakwater to Partridge Island is not to take place. From all I can learn, it is very doubtful whether it would be of any advantage, and certainly it would be productive of many disadvantages, which are quite manifest. Does the amount that it will cost to keep the ' Fielding ' at work straightening the channel come out of this vote ?
No, that comes out of the general dredging vote.

I asked the minister a question the other day relative to the importation at St. John from the United States of a dredge which was employed on this work. Does that dredge belong to what
is known as the Dominion Dredging Company of Ottawa, of which Mr. Gordon Stewart is secretary treasurer ?
That is a dredge belonging to the Dominion Dredging Company of Ottawa. I do not know whether Mr. Stewart is secretary treasurer of the company or not.
Is the kon. gentleman aware that Mr. Stewart is connected with the company in some capacity ?
My impression is that he is president of the company.
Under what circumstances was that dredge admitted free of duty ?
In the answer which I gave to my hon. friend I stated that duty to the extent of $26,000 had been paid on it. So I was informed by the Commissioner of Customs.
May I ask what work has been performed by this dredge at St. John, how much has the Dominion Dredging Company been paid by the government in all, and what period of time did that cover ?	.
The answer I gave to my hon. friend on July 2nd contains the full information.

Were tenders called
for the work which was allotted to this Dominion Dredging Company ?
Yes.

How many tenders
were received V

There was only one tender received-from Mr. G. S. Mayes, at 90 cents per cubic yard. It then became necessary, in the judgment of the people of St. John who took an interest in the work, and in the judgment of the minister, to put on an additional dredge ; the minister was pressed very strongly to do that, in order to have the dredging done, for the purpose of building a wharf with a warehouse upon it, for the purpose of accommodating the ocean steamers. As a result of that, the Dominion Dredging Company, having offered to take a part of the work at the same price as Mr. Mayes' tender, was given the work at that price, namely, 90 cents per cubic yard.
Did you take the work away from Mr. Mayes ?
No, he continued to do his work.

As I have paid some little attention to these dredging matters, I must congratulate the Dominion Dredging Company on its departure from the province of Ontario to larger and greener pas-

tures in the province of the Minister of Public Works, namely, New Brunswick, and, if all reports are true as to the financial success of the Dominion Dredging Company at St. John, they will never regret the day they went there. It is a political organization, there is no doubt about that. The company is well known in the city of Ottawa. That Mr. Stewart, who is the secretary treasurer of the company-the minister says he is the president, but I rather think he is mistaken in that, because in the tenders Mr. Stewart signs himself as secretary treasurer-has a strong political pull, goes without saying, because he is a son of the senior member for Ottawa. In the city of St. John there is published a paper which though friendly to this administration is not friendly to the Minister of Public Works. I refer to the St. John ' Globe.' That paper which is owned and edited by Senator Ellis, a lifelong Liberal, has made some caustic comments on these dredging operations in the harbour of St. John. The person who writes the articles in that newspaper is evidently thoroughly conversant with all the facts. I have some figures taken from that newspaper which are all borne out by the figures given by the hon. minister in his answer to the question of July 2nd. It would appear that at one time Mr. Mayes had a contract for dredging in St. John harbour at a certain figure. The bulk of the material is paid for at the rate of 90 cents per cubic yard. There were no tenders called publicly for this work.
My hon. friend is in error. Tenders were called for by advertisement published in the newspapers.
Do I understand that two tenders were received ?
No, only one tender, that of Mr. G. S. Mayes, at 90 cents per cubic yard.

That is the statement I was coming to. Mayes had a tender in, but the Dominion Dredging Company did not tender at all. For reasons best known to himself, the minister gave the contract to that company at the same figure at which Mayes tendered.
You mean my predecessor, Mr. Fisher, who was acting minister.
I thought it was the hon. gentleman himself. Was the contract closed by Mr. Fisher while acting minister?
Yes, I suppose if the editor of the St. John ' Globe ' had known that, he would not have been so critical.

It may be that Senator Ellis' knowledge of the hon. gentleman makes him critical of anything done in any department controlled by him. I leave the hon. minister and Senator Ellis to settle their own differences and let the warring Mr. BENNETT.
factions fight it out. That article goes on to point out the quantities taken out, and the result was that there was altogether earned the sum of about $375,000 by ttis dredge. At the same time it earned a considerable amount from the city of (St. John, but of course that is a private matter with which we have nothing to do.
Where do you find that statement?
In the article in the St. John ' Globe.'

My hon. friend from the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel) will not say that is correct. Will he say that the Dominion Dredging Company, in addition to doing work for the Dominion government earned considerable from the city of St. John?
No doubt the city of St. John paid the sum of $25,000 for dredging.
That was to Mr. G. S. Mayes and was paid to the city by my department. It was not paid to the Dominion Dredging Company at all.
In addition to the $375,000, there was work amounting to $18,000 done for the department on what is known as the long wharf. By whom was that done?
That is included in the $375,000.

Then there was $375,000 earned in all on what is known as * other material ' at 90 cents a yard. What amount was earned by this company for the removal of the boulders? Or was that included in the $375,000?
Yes.

The accounts show that this favoured company had earned about $375,000 in its dealings with the department at St. John. It is stated by persons conversant with the facts that this dredge, together with the duty, cost the Dominion Company, $140,000. It was publicly stated in a St. John newspaper that after she was brought from the United States, $15,000 was expended on her for repairs. The time during which she earned' this amount was a period of about ten months and the running expenses $8,000 per month. Allowing for the towage and insurance while in transit from the United States to St. John, amounting to $3,000, the total cost was about $238,000. The dredge earned $375,000 making a net profit to the owners of about $137,000, so that these fortunate contractors have in ten months made a net profit of about $137,000 and have the dredge in the bargain. Is it not about time the department woke up to one of two things. Either to buy the dredges themselves or else invite more competition; and if compe-

tition is not forthcoming, then simply tell the dredge owners that the department is not prepared to pay those prices. It seems to me a startling state of affairs that such huge profits should be made by the dredge owners. These figures come from an impartial source because I assume that Senator Ellis is looked upon as fairly trustworthy.
Does my hon. friend say that these figures, which he has given of the running expenses and cost of the dredge were given by Senator Ellis?
No.
The figures as to the amount paid were given in the answer I gave the other day.
Quite true, but the hon. gentleman has not yet given any figures as to the cost of the dredge.
And you say that Senator Ellis has not given you that.
I say that his newspaper has given some of the figures.
Did it give the cost of the dredging and running expenses?
No, that is a computation by parties who are in a position to speak with authority.
Will You give the names?

Is the hon. gentleman always so generous himself? Has he not time and again been asked to give the names of his informants when he made some very damaging statements concerning the leader of the opposition and has he not always been as silent as the tomb?
If the leader of the opposition asks me to give the name of my informants regarding anything I have said concerning him, I shall be glad to accomodate him.
I do not propose to give the names of my informants. May I ask the minister what is the estimate of his department as to the value of the dredge?

We have nothing to do with the value of the dredge. According to my information, it is a most efficient dredge, of splendid working capacity, and has been well managed, and is one of the very best in the Dominion.
What is the size of the scoop?-I do not mean the owner's scoop but the scoop of the dredge?

Seven cubic yards to each bucket. Surely when tenders were called for by public advertisement, the department performed its full duty. These tenders were advertised in various newspapers and all reasonable means taken for the securing of tenders.
What newspapers?
I cannot give the names now-the ordinary newspapers in which advertisements of this kind are published.
Party newspapers?
Newspapers having large circulation. I will give the names, but cannot do so to-night.
The circulation of the party newspapers in New Brunswick is very limited.

My hon. friend has suggested that the Dominion Dredging Company got this work because they were favoured contractors. That statement has no foundation. Tenders were publicly called for and Mr. G, S. Mayes was the only one who tendered. His price was 90 cents per cubic yard.
Was the minister forced to accept just one tender?
He was not, but on the advice of the cnief engineer, and knowing what was being paid elsewhere, the minister concluded that a new call for tenders would have the same result.
What was the date of Mr. Mayes' tender ?
It was September 21, 1906.
And there was only one tender ?
Yes.

I do not understand that. If the minister will refer to 1 Hansard ' of June 29, he will find reference to dredging at Sand Point and Rodney slips, and there were two tenders, those of Mr. Mayes and Haney & Miller.

I am glad the hon. gentleman called attention to that. That was the first tender in 1905. Mr. Mayes tendered at 55 cents, and Messrs. Haney & Miller, who are experienced contractors and men of the highest reputation and the best judgment, tendered at $1. Mr. Mayes would gladly have got rid of his contract afterwards, as he says it has been a losing contract to him, but we have held him to it. New tenders were called for the further work by public advertisement, and for that there was only one tender.
Of what figure ?

Ninety cents, which is still 10 cents lower than that of Haney & Miller. A little later, while Mr. Fisher was acting minister, a feeling arose that Mr. Mayes could not get the work done in time and that two dredges were necessary. In the meantime, having performed a portion

of the work upon the north side of the slip, he had been set at work further down. Under extreme and urgent pressure by the people of St. John, the minister gave the Dominion Dredging Company an opportunity to join in that work at the same price at which Mr. Mayes had tendered.
When the additional work was ordered, were tenders asked for ? Or was Mr. Mayes asked what he would do the work for ?
No, for he was doing the work at 90 cents. Later, when I became minister, further work was required, and X divided up the work, as well as I could, between the two at the rate tendered.
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) will excuse me, there was no ' dividing up '. He gave the additional work without calling for tenders or asking the first tenderer what he would do it for.
The first tenderer could not do it. He had only one dredge, and two dredges were required.
Was Mr. Mayes informed that he would be permitted to import a dredge from the United States to engage in the work ?

I do not know. But I do happen to know that Mr. Mayes was allowed the same privilege-he brought in his dredge from the United States and paid his duty, I think, in instalments. And I understood that when he got through he was going to return it. Now, when we wanted to get dredging done on the western side of the Long Wharf, I directed the chief engineer to ask for tenders from these two companies. The Dominion Dredging Company tendered at 90 cents and Mr. Mayes at $1.10. The contract was made with the Dominion Dredging Company. Now, dredging in St. John harbour is very difficult as compared with dredging in non-tidal *waters or in waters where the tide rises only four or five feet.
That tender of Mr. Mayes was $1.10 for clay. Were there not other figures for the other classes of material 1
I do not know, but that would not affect the case because no rock or boulders were found west of the Long Wharf.
It would affect the acceptance of tenders. The tender of these people would be a good deal higher for boulders and rock and that of the other man higher for clay.
Yes. But the tender with respect to boulders would not affect the contract which was for other material; It turned out to be all clav. In St.

John harbour the tide rises 25 feet and the dredging has to be done 60 feet below high water. So, it frequently happens, unless the work can be so laid out as to keep the dredges going in both high and low water, that the dredge will be idle during the high water. Mr. Mayes' dredge was frequently Idle, and he complained that he was obliged to lose a great deal of time. The department cannot be responsible for what the Dominion Dredging Company made or did not make. I have reason to believe that the acting minister was in no way influenced by whether that company was friendly or not. I do not know that he was acquainted with the members of it, but in any case it made no difference. The citizens of St. John had urgently requested that two dredges be employed to complete the work as speedily as possible. And, as I say, all this was done before I became minister. Tenders were called for in the most open manner. If we proceed under this vote, my intention is to call for tenders publicly, so that the work may be done as cheaply as possible.

Was it contemplated by the minister, when either Mr. Ayles-worth or Mr. Fisher was acting minister, that the same dredge that was purchased by the Dominion Dredging Company should be purchased by the department ? Is it true that a gentleman connected with the department inspected the dredge and got a price on it ?
I do not know of my own knowledge, but I am informed by my deputy that that is not the case.

Has the minister taken into consideration the purchasing of a dredge as part of this expenditure of $400,000 ? Considering the statement of the hon. member for East Simcoe, that the dredge in ten months earned its own price and $155,000 besides, might it not be worth the minister's while to consider the purchasing of a dredge to do the work there that is required from year to year ?

That is an important question. There is no doubt that the dredging company had good luck, with no breakdowns to speak of, and they had this splendid dredge. We have a number of dredges in the maritime provinces and we have some in Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia.
